topic: Planning compass-and-straightedge constructions and justifying them
subtitle: Planning classical compass-straightedge constructions and justifications

problems.desc: Rubric for the plan. A full-credit plan draws a ray from the new starting point, sets the compass to the exact span of the given segment without changing it, places the compass point on the new endpoint and strikes an arc across the ray, and marks the crossing as the far endpoint. Three moves must be present: set the span, transfer it unchanged, mark the crossing. Deduct for any step that measures with a ruler, since the compass is what guarantees the copy is congruent.

Rubric for the justification of the perpendicular bisector. A full-credit answer says that both arcs were drawn with the same compass setting, so each of the two crossing points is the same distance from one endpoint as from the other; that makes each crossing point equidistant from the two endpoints, and the line through two such points is the perpendicular bisector. Accept the congruent-triangles version: the four equal radii and the shared side give two congruent triangles by side-side-side, so the angles at the crossing are congruent and supplementary, hence right. No credit for describing the drawing again without saying why equal radii force the result.

Rubric for the angle-bisector plan. A full-credit plan places the compass at the vertex and strikes one arc crossing both sides of the angle, then from each of those two crossings strikes arcs of equal radius that meet inside the angle, then draws the ray from the vertex through that meeting point. The answer must also say what each arc guarantees: the first arc marks two points the same distance from the vertex, and the second pair marks a point the same distance from each of those, which is what makes the two halves congruent by side-side-side. Deduct for a plan that produces the ray but never says what the equal radii buy.

Rubric for the written conclusion. A full-credit answer says the two distances are equal, so the point is equidistant from the two endpoints, and that every such point lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Accept an answer that adds the converse statement of the perpendicular bisector theorem in its own words. No credit for repeating the two distances with no statement about where the point must lie.

Rubric for the copy-an-angle justification. A full-credit answer identifies the two triangles formed by the arc crossings and the vertices, notes that the first arc was struck with one radius on both angles so two pairs of sides are congruent, and that the second compass span was carried over unchanged so the third pair is congruent, giving congruence by side-side-side; the copied angle is then congruent as a matching part. Accept an answer that names the three congruent pairs and the criterion without naming the parts formally. No credit for restating the steps of the construction with no congruence criterion.

Rubric for the parallel-line plan. A full-credit plan draws a transversal through the given point meeting the given line, copies the angle that the transversal makes with the given line to the same side at the given point, and draws the line along the copied ray. The answer must name the theorem that finishes it: congruent corresponding angles force the two lines to be parallel. Accept alternate interior angles if the copy is placed on the other side. Deduct for a plan that only says draw a parallel line, and for one that omits the theorem.

(b) the distance from the centre to the image

problems.desc: Rubric for the written conclusion. A full-credit answer divides the second distance by the first, gets three, and says that a dilation multiplies every distance from the centre by the scale factor, which is why the ratio recovers it. It should also note that the centre, the point and its image are collinear. Accept an answer that shows the ratio and states the scale factor without the collinearity remark, at reduced credit.

Rubric for the equilateral-triangle construction. A full-credit plan strikes an arc centred at each endpoint of the given segment, both with the compass set to the whole segment, and joins either crossing point to the two endpoints. The justification must say that the two arcs have the same radius as the segment, so the two new sides are each congruent to it, and therefore to each other, which makes all three sides congruent. Deduct for a plan with the right drawing and no radius argument.

problems.desc: Rubric for the square-construction plan. A full-credit plan names the earlier constructions it reuses: erect a perpendicular to the given segment at each endpoint, transfer the segment length up each perpendicular with the compass, and join the two new points. Any plan that reaches a square through a stated sequence of the constructions on this sheet earns full credit; a plan that names no earlier construction does not.

Rubric for the square justification. A full-credit answer gives both halves: all four sides are congruent because the compass span was never changed, and all four angles are right because the two perpendiculars were constructed as perpendiculars and the fourth angle then follows from the angle sum of a quadrilateral. An answer that argues only equal sides has built a rhombus, not a square, and earns half credit; say so on the paper.
